If ye, legalists, must "bear burdens," then instead of legal burdens (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.4">Mt 23:4</reference>), "bear one another's burdens," literally, "weights." Distinguished by Bengel from "burden," <reference osisRef="Gal.6.4">Ga 6:4</reference> (a different Greek word, "load"): "weights" exceed the strength of those under them; "burden" is proportioned to the strength.<div eID="gen35293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35294" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so fulfil--</hi>or as other old manuscripts read, "so ye will fulfil," Greek, "fill up," "thoroughly fulfil."<div eID="gen35294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35295" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the law of Christ--</hi>namely, "love" (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.14">Ga 5:14</reference>). Since ye desire "the law," then fulfil the law of Christ, which is not made up of various minute observances, but whose sole "burden" is "love" (<reference osisRef="John.13.34">Joh 13:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.12">15:12</reference>); <reference osisRef="Rom.15.3">Ro 15:3</reference> gives Christ as the example in the particular duty here. <div eID="gen35295" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17556"/><div sID="gen35300" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17556"/><hi type="bold">4. his own work--</hi>not merely his own opinion of himself.<div eID="gen35300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35301" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have rejoicing in himself alone--</hi>Translate, "Have his (matter for) glorying in regard to himself alone, and not in regard to another (namely, not in regard to his neighbor, by comparing himself with whom, he has fancied he has matter for boasting as that neighbor's superior)." Not that really a man by looking to "himself alone" is likely to find cause for glorying in himself. Nay, in <reference osisRef="Gal.6.5">Ga 6:5</reference>, he speaks of a "burden" or load, not of matter for glorying, as what really belongs to each man. But he refers to the idea those whom he censures had of themselves: they thought they had cause for "glorying" in themselves, but it all arose from unjust self-conceited comparison of themselves with others, instead of looking at home. The only true glorying, if glorying it is to be called, is in the testimony of a good conscience, glorying in the cross of Christ. <div eID="gen35301" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17557"/><div sID="gen35302" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17557"/>5. For (by this way, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.4">Ga 6:4</reference>, of proving himself, not depreciating his neighbor by comparison) each man shall bear his own "burden," or rather, "load" (namely, of sin and infirmity), the Greek being different from that in <reference osisRef="Gal.6.2">Ga 6:2</reference>. This verse does not contradict <reference osisRef="Gal.6.2">Ga 6:2</reference>. There he tells them to bear with others' "burdens" of infirmity in sympathy; here, that self-examination will make a man to feel he has enough to do with "his own load" of sin, without comparing himself boastfully with his neighbor. Compare <reference osisRef="Gal.6.3">Ga 6:3</reference>. Instead of "thinking himself to be something," he shall feel the "load" of his own sin: and this will lead him to bear sympathetically with his neighbor's burden of infirmity. ÆSOP says a man carries two bags over his shoulder, the one with his own sins hanging behind, that with his neighbor's sins in front. <div eID="gen35302" type="x-p"/>

God is not mocked--</hi>The Greek verb is, literally, to sneer with the nostrils drawn up in contempt. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17560"/><div sID="gen35310" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17560"/>8. Translate, "He that soweth unto his own flesh," with a view to fulfilling its desires. He does not say, "His spirit," as he does say, "His flesh." For in ourselves we are not spiritual, but carnal. The flesh is devoted to selfishness.<div eID="gen35310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35311" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">corruption--</hi>that is, destruction (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Php 3:19</reference>). Compare as to the deliverance of believers from "corruption" (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.21">Ro 8:21</reference>). The use of the term "corruption" instead, implies that destruction is not an arbitrary punishment of fleshly-mindedness, but is its natural fruit; the corrupt flesh producing corruption, which is another word for destruction: corruption is the fault, and corruption the punishment (see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.17">1Co 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.12">2Pe 2:12</reference>). Future life only expands the seed sown here. Men cannot mock God because they can deceive themselves. They who sow tares cannot reap wheat. They alone reap life eternal who sow to the Spirit (<reference osisRef="Ps.126.6">Psa 126:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.11.18">Pr 11:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.8">22:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.7">Ho 8:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.10.12">10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.16.25">Lu 16:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.11">Ro 8:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.7">Jas 5:7</reference>). <div eID="gen35311" type="x-p"/>

Translate, "So then, according as (that is, in proportion as) we have season (that is, opportunity), let us work (a distinct Greek verb from that for "do," in <reference osisRef="Gal.6.9">Ga 6:9</reference>) that which is (in each case) good." entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17563"/><div sID="gen35317" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17563"/>11. Rather, "See in how large letters I have written." The Greek is translated "how great" in <reference osisRef="Heb.7.4">He 7:4</reference>, the only other passage where it occurs in the New Testament. Owing to his weakness of eyes (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.15">Ga 4:15</reference>) he wrote in large letters. So Jerome. All the oldest manuscripts are written in uncial, that is, capital letters, the "cursive," or small letters, being of more recent date. Paul seems to have had a difficulty in writing, which led him to make the uncial letters larger than ordinary writers did. The mention of these is as a token by which they would know that he wrote the whole Epistle with his own hand; as he did also the pastoral Epistle, which this Epistle resembles in style. He usually dictated his Epistles to an amanuensis, excepting the concluding salutation, which he wrote himself (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.22">Ro 16:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.21">1Co 16:21</reference>). This letter, he tells the Galatians, he writes with his own hand, no doubt in order that they may see what a regard he had for them, in contrast to the Judaizing teachers (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.12">Ga 6:12</reference>), who sought only their own ease. If English Version be retained, the words, "how large a letter (literally, 'in how large letters')," will not refer to the length of the Epistle absolutely, but that it was a large one for him to have written with his own hand. Neander supports English Version, as more appropriate to the earnestness of the apostle and the tone of the Epistle: "How large" will thus be put for "how many." <div eID="gen35317" type="x-p"/>
